units.title: Basics 1
units.description: Learn your very first Japanese words and simple sentences using です (to be), たべます (to eat), and のみます (to drink).
units.guidebook:
Welcome to Japanese! 🎌

**People & things**
- 男の人 (おとこのひと) means "man" and 女の人 (おんなのひと) means "woman." For kids, use 男の子 (おとこのこ, boy) and 女の子 (おんなのこ, girl).
- りんご (apple) and パン (bread) are written in hiragana and katakana — Japanese uses both!
- みず (water) and ぎゅうにゅう (milk) are everyday drinks.

**The verb です (desu)**
です is like "am/is/are." Attach it to a noun: りんご**です** = "It is an apple." To say "I am a student," use わたしは がくせいです.

**Eating & drinking**
- たべます (tabemasu) = "eat" → りんごを たべます = "I eat an apple."
- のみます (nomimasu) = "drink" → みずを のみます = "I drink water."

**Particles**
- は marks the topic ("as for me…").
- を marks the object of an action.

Try reading each phrase out loud! がんばって!

units.title: Greetings
units.description: Learn essential Japanese greetings and polite expressions for everyday interactions.
units.guidebook:
# Greetings in Japanese 🇯🇵

Japanese greetings are deeply tied to **politeness levels**. The most common casual hello is **こんにちは** (konnichiwa), used mainly in the afternoon. In the morning, say **おはようございます** (ohayou gozaimasu), and at night use **こんばんは** (konbanwa).

When meeting someone for the first time or in formal settings, use **はじめまして** (hajimemashite), meaning "Nice to meet you," often followed by your name and **よろしくお願いします** (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), a versatile phrase meaning "Please treat me well."

**Politeness matters!** Adding **です** (desu) or **ます** (masu) makes sentences polite. For example, **ありがとう** (arigatou) is casual "thanks," while **ありがとうございます** is the polite form.

**Goodbyes** include **さようなら** (sayounara), often used for longer farewells, and **じゃあね** (jaa ne) for casual "see you." **おやすみなさい** (oyasuminasai) means "good night."

Remember: bowing slightly while greeting shows respect! 🙇

units.title: Food
units.description: Learn essential Japanese words for common foods and drinks, plus how to say you want to eat and drink them.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to the Food unit! 🍱

In this unit, you'll learn common food and drink vocabulary. Japanese nouns don't have articles like "a" or "the," so コーヒー means both "coffee" and "the coffee."

**Wanting things** uses the verb ほしい (hoshii). To say "I want coffee," say コーヒーがほしい (kōhī ga hoshii). The particle **が (ga)** marks what you want.

**Eating and drinking** use 食べる (taberu, "to eat") and 飲む (nomu, "to drink"). To say "I eat rice," use ごはんをたべる (gohan o taberu). The particle **を (o)** marks the direct object.

**Polite form**: Adding ます (masu) makes sentences polite. のみます (nomimasu) = "drink (polite)."

**Word order** is Subject + Object + Verb: わたしはパンをたべます (Watashi wa pan o tabemasu) = "I eat bread."

Enjoy your meal — itadakimasu! 🍣

units.title: Animals
units.description: Learn the names of common animals in Japanese and how to describe them with simple sentences.
units.guidebook:
## Animals in Japanese 🐾

Welcome to the animal unit! In Japanese, animal names are written in **katakana** when borrowed from other languages, and in **kanji** or **hiragana** for native Japanese words.

### Key Patterns

**Saying "It is a ___":**
Use the plain form: **犬です** (inu desu) — "It is a dog."

**Describing animals with adjectives:**
- **大きい** (ookii) — big
- **小さい** (chiisai) — small
- **可愛い** (kawaii) — cute

Example: **猫は可愛いです** (neko wa kawaii desu) — "The cat is cute."

### Useful Particles

- **は** (wa) — topic marker: "as for the ___..."
- **が** (ga) — subject marker, often used with descriptive sentences

### Animal Sounds 🐶
Japanese has fun onomatopoeia for animal sounds:
- Dogs: **ワンワン** (wan wan)
- Cats: **ニャーニャー** (nyaa nyaa)
- Birds: **ピーピー** (pii pii)

Try combining what you know: **鳥は小さいです** (tori wa chiisai desu) — "The bird is small." Happy learning!

units.title: Travel
units.description: Learn essential Japanese vocabulary and phrases for navigating cities, trains, hotels, airports, and asking for directions.
units.guidebook:
## Travel in Japanese 🚆

This unit covers the basics of getting around Japan. You'll learn vocabulary for transportation, places, and asking for help.

### Key Grammar Points

**は (wa) - Topic marker:** Marks the topic of a sentence. Example: 駅はどこですか (Eki wa doko desu ka) - "Where is the station?"

**を (wo) - Object marker:** Used with motion verbs. Example: バスに乗ります (Basu ni norimasu) - "I ride the bus."

**に (ni) - Direction/Destination:** Indicates where you're going. Example: ホテルに行きます (Hoteru ni ikimasu) - "I go to the hotel."

**どこ (doko) - Where:** Combine with desu ka to ask "where is ___?"

### Useful Patterns

- ___はどこですか? - "Where is ___?"
- ___に行きます - "I'm going to ___."
- ___をください - "Please give me ___" (when ordering)

### Travel Tips 🗾

Japan has an incredible train system. When asking for directions, politeness goes a long way. Adding すみません (sumimasen) before a question is the standard way to get attention.

units.title: Family
units.description: Learn how to talk about your family members, siblings, and relatives in Japanese.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Family in Japanese

In Japanese, the words you use for family members often depend on whose family you are discussing!

When talking about your own family to others, use humble terms: **chichi** (father), **haha** (mother), **ani** (older brother), and **ane** (older sister). This shows politeness by lowering your own circle.

When talking about someone else's family or calling out to your own relatives directly, polite forms are used instead, like **otousan** (father) and **okaasan** (mother).

Additionally, Japanese specifies age among siblings: **ani** and **ane** for older siblings, and **otouto** (younger brother) and **imouto** (younger sister) for younger ones.

exercises.translation: My older brother is in Tokyo.

alternatives: Watashi ni wa imouto ga imasu.

units.title: Shopping
units.description: Learn to ask for prices, talk about shops, and buy items in Japanese.
units.guidebook:
### Essential Shopping Phrases

When browsing stores in Japan, your most powerful question is **これはいくらですか** (*Kore wa ikura desu ka?* — "How much is this?"). 

### Prices and Currency
Japanese currency is measured in **円** (*en*, pronounced "yen"). Simply attach the number before 円, such as **千円** (*sen'en*, 1,000 yen) or **百円** (*hyaku'en*, 100 yen).

### Describing Value
Use the *-i* adjectives **高い** (*takai* — expensive) and **安い** (*yasui* — cheap). Add **です** (*desu*) to make polite statements: **これは高いです** (*Kore wa takai desu* — "This is expensive").

### At the Register
Cashiers often ask if you need a bag (**袋**, *fukuro*). You can request items politely by adding **をお願いします** (*o onegai shimasu*): **レシートをお願いします** (*Reshīto o onegai shimasu* — "The receipt, please").

units.title: Weather
units.description: Learn to talk about the weather, seasons, and daily climate in Japanese.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About the Weather

Discussing the weather is the ultimate Japanese icebreaker! Keep these handy tips in mind:

#### Hot vs. Cold
Japanese distinguishes between ambient air temperature and physical touch:
- **暑い** (*atsui*) means hot weather, while **寒い** (*samui*) means cold weather.
- For things you touch (like a hot tea or an iced drink), use **熱い** (*atsui*) and **冷たい** (*tsumetai*) instead.

#### Precipitation
To express that rain or snow is falling, use the verb **降る** (*furu*, to fall):
- **雨が降ります** (*ame ga furimasu*) = It rains.
- **雪が降っています** (*yuki ga futte imasu*) = It is snowing.

Wrap up friendly observations with **ね** (*ne*), as in **いい天気ですね** (*Nice weather, isn't it?*).

units.title: Work & School
units.description: Talk about jobs, workplaces, school life, and daily tasks in Japanese.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to Work & School! Here you will learn how to discuss careers, classes, and daily study habits.

### Talking About Professions
To state someone's occupation, use the basic sentence frame: **[Person] は [Profession] です** (*[Person] wa [Profession] desu*). For example: 私は学生です (*Watashi wa gakusei desu* – "I am a student").

### The Honorific Title 先生 (*Sensei*)
**先生** is an honorific title reserved for teachers, doctors, and authors. Address your teacher as *Tanaka-sensei*, never *Tanaka-san*! When describing your own profession, avoid calling yourself *sensei*; instead, use 医者 (*isha*) for doctor or 教師 (*kyoushi*) for teacher.

### Location of Action: Particle で (*de*)
Use the particle **で** to mark the place where an activity happens: 病院**で**働きます (*Byouin de hatarakimasu* – "I work at a hospital").

units.title: Health
units.description: Learn words and phrases for talking about your body, sickness, and medical care.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Aches and Pains
When expressing physical pain in Japanese, state the body part, add the subject particle **が (ga)**, and finish with **痛い (itai)**. For example, **頭が痛いです (atama ga itai desu)** means "My head hurts."

### Essential Health Phrases
* **Taking medicine:** Japanese uses the verb **飲む (nomu)** meaning "to drink" for pills and medicine: **薬を飲む (kusuri o nomu)**.
* **Catching a cold:** Use the fixed expression **風邪をひく (kaze o hiku)**. When you already caught one, say **風邪をひきました (kaze o hikimashita)**.
* **Being tired:** Exhaustion is usually expressed in the past tense: **疲れました (tsukaremashita)**, literally "I have become tired."
